claims.text: Matching, fast-decomposing precursor ligands promote synchronous release of all metal species.
Synchronous metal release causes simultaneous nucleation.
Simultaneous nucleation locks the nanoparticles into a uniform, single-phase solid solution.
Staggered ligand decomposition produces transient local concentration variations.
Transient local concentration variations favor phase separation and elemental segregation.
Ligand decomposition kinetics govern whether nucleation is synchronized or unsynchronized.
Rapid simultaneous metal release creates a high and spatially uniform metal concentration.
A high, uniform metal concentration triggers collective nucleation.
Collective nucleation leads to a homogeneous single-phase crystal structure.
Staggered precursor decomposition creates nonuniform metal availability and localized differences in nucleation timing.
Matching, fast-decomposing ligands will yield more homogeneous elemental distributions and a single-phase crystal structure.
Staggered ligand decomposition will yield phase segregation, elemental inhomogeneity, and irregular particle morphology.
Rapid heating and cooling with standard precursor ligands typically produces phase-separated and compositionally inhomogeneous nanoparticles.
The proposed intervention applies to noble-metal HEA nanoparticles containing more than five elements under rapid thermal processing.
The intervention's effectiveness depends on ligand chemistry and ligand decomposition profiles.
Solvent effects, precursor concentration, and secondary interactions during growth may also influence the final phase.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome refers to comparison with a 'single-phase baseline,' whereas the explicitly defined baseline is phase-separated and compositionally inhomogeneous.
